name: Jehangir Art Gallery
overview: Exhibition gallery at 161 Kala Ghoda in the Fort area of South Mumbai, beside the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya, formerly the Prince of Wales Museum (gallery site).

Founded by Sir Cowasji Jehangir, 2nd Baronet (1879 to 1962), an industrialist and banker, in memory of his late son Jehangir; B. G. Kher, then Chief Minister of Bombay, inaugurated it on 21 January 1952 (gallery site). Wikipedia says he founded it at the urging of K. K. Hebbar and Homi J. Bhabha.
The gallery site credits the architect Durga Bajpai; Wikipedia's introduction credits G. M. Bhuta, tagged "citation needed", while its architecture section also names Bajpai.
funding_verdict: Jehangir Art Gallery: run by a committee on the Jehangir family's founding gift, with exhibitors' fees
wider_context: April 2013: after complaints, Mumbai police and the gallery insisted, the artist said, that Eleena Banik remove two goddess paintings from public view, one of Kali without her garland of skulls and one she said protested the Delhi gang rape; Varsha Thakar of the Hindu Janajagruti Samiti was among the complainants, Banik received a death threat and police protection, and director K. G. Menon confirmed the request (AFP via The National, 11 April 2013).

December 2007: two policemen visited Jatin Das's show and suggested barring under-18s; Joint Police Commissioner K. L. Prasad called it a suggestion, and Das put up a "Not Under 18" notice. The year before, the gallery had asked a student to cover parts of a nude sculpture (Subir Ghosh, blog, citing Hindustan Times).

name: Selasar Sunaryo Art Space
overview: Non-profit art space at Jalan Bukit Pakar Timur 100, Ciburial, Cimenyan, Bandung Regency, in the Dago area (CNN Indonesia, 2017; detikJabar, 2024; culture360).

Founded by the artist Sunaryo, a former lecturer at the art and design faculty of the Bandung Institute of Technology, and opened on 5 September 1998 (detikJabar). Director General of Culture Edi Setyawati opened it (CNN Indonesia, 2017).
The first show, "Titik Nadir", covered Sunaryo's works in black cloth, which Manual calls "a sombre expression of the grief and uncertainty" of the turmoil of the time.
funding_verdict: Selasar Sunaryo Art Space: self-funded: the founder's land and building, with his foundation's support, run by his family

press_items.title: Tanya Michele Amador, "Selasar Sunaryo Art Space in Bandung Turns 20" (2018)
Anindito Ariwandono, "Reconnecting with earth at Leuwigoèng" (2022)

name: The Glucksman
overview: Contemporary art museum in the lower grounds of University College Cork (UCC). It is run by ArtGallery (UCC) DAC, a designated activity company whose registered office is UCC's Secretary's Office (the company's 2025 annual report).
Opened on 14 October 2004 by President Mary McAleese (the museum's history page). Formerly called the Lewis Glucksman Gallery. Fiona Kearney was its inaugural director (Wikipedia).

Named for Lewis Glucksman, one of its founding donors, whom the museum calls an American financier and philanthropist. Wikipedia describes him as a Wall Street financier and chairman of Lehman Brothers, Kuhn, Loeb Inc.
funding_verdict: The Glucksman: mainly public: University College Cork subvention and the Arts Council, with small earned income

name: Douglas Hyde Gallery
overview: Contemporary art gallery in the Arts Building of Trinity College Dublin, on the campus in central Dublin.

Co-founded by the Arts Council of Ireland and Trinity College Dublin. Opened to the public on 1 March 1978 as the first publicly funded contemporary art exhibition space in Ireland (gallery website). Wikipedia describes it as Ireland's first university gallery.
Named after Douglas Hyde, the first President of Ireland (gallery website). Wikipedia calls him a Trinity graduate.
funding_verdict: Douglas Hyde Gallery: publicly supported: the Arts Council and Trinity College Dublin, with private patrons

name: Hugh Lane Gallery
overview: Municipal gallery of modern and contemporary art at Charlemont House, Parnell Square North, Dublin 1, operated by Dublin City Council and its wholly owned company, the Hugh Lane Gallery Trust (Wikipedia).
Founded by Sir Hugh Lane, who opened it on Harcourt Street on 20 January 1908 and paid its running costs (Wikipedia). It has been in Charlemont House since 1933 (Wikipedia).

Named for Lane, who died in 1915 when the RMS Lusitania sank. His will left his collection to London, but an unwitnessed codicil gave 39 paintings to Dublin. A 1959 compromise split the bequest between the two cities, and a 1993 change kept 31 paintings in Ireland (Wikipedia). Under a 2021 partnership, 39 bequest paintings are shared with the National Gallery, London (Dublin City Council).
funding_verdict: Hugh Lane Gallery: public: Dublin City Council

name: Design Museum Holon
overview: Design museum at Pinchas Ayalon 8 in Holon.
Opened in March 2010 in a building designed by Ron Arad Architects.
Holon mayor Moti Sasson and the city's managing director Hana Hertsman directed the commission for the building (museum About page).
funding_verdict: Design Museum Holon: municipal: the Holon municipality
wider_context: Curator Mia Dvash resigned amid tensions and disagreements between Holon's cultural institutions and the municipality (Ynet, Dar Moussafir).
Those tensions led to the closure or downsizing of several city institutions, among them the Center for Puppetry and the Center for Digital Art, whose head Udi Edelman resigned.

For the exhibition "The Circle: Designing New Realities", some international designers declined to take part. Cohen Mordechai told Ynet that some creators worried how the international design community would view an exhibition in Israel.
The museum is funded by the same municipality that cut its sister institutions.

name: MAMbo
overview: Municipal museum of modern and contemporary art at Via Don Minzoni 14, Bologna, part of the city's civic museums (Bologna Welcome).
Opened on 5 May 2007 in the former municipal bakery, built in 1915 under mayor Francesco Zanardi. A redevelopment designed by Aldo Rossi turned it into the museum (Finestre sull'Arte, 6 May 2020).
It grew out of Bologna's Galleria d'Arte Moderna, founded in 1925, and became a separate entity in the 1990s. Wikipedia says it was rebranded "MAMbo" and moved into the former bakery.
funding_verdict: MAMbo: mixed: the City of Bologna's transfer to Istituzione Bologna Musei, slightly under half of its revenue, plus own revenue

press_items.title: Redazione, "Ecco come è successo che Gianfranco Maraniello è di nuovo direttore del Mambo. Anzi di tutti i Musei Bolognesi: a Vittorio Sgarbi piacendo. Storia travagliata di un rinnovo" (15 September 2013)

name: Museion
overview: Museum of modern and contemporary art in Bolzano, South Tyrol, at Piazza Piero Siena 1 (Museion activity report 2021).
Founded in 1985 by the Associazione Museion. It began operating in 1987 in the former hospital building on via Sernesi (Museion website).
Became a private-law foundation in 2006, with the Autonomous Province of Bolzano-South Tyrol and the Museion Private Founders as its founders (Museion website).
funding_verdict: Museion: mainly public: the Autonomous Province of Bolzano, with small shares from the ministry, a bank foundation, tickets and sponsors

name: Castello di Rivoli
overview: Contemporary art museum in the former Savoy castle at Piazza Mafalda di Savoia, Rivoli, Turin. From Turin, visitors take the metro to Paradiso, then bus 36 and a shuttle bus to the museum (Castello di Rivoli).

The castle reopened in 1984 as the Museo d'Arte Contemporanea, described by Wikipedia as the first contemporary art museum in Italy. Rudi Fuchs and Johannes Gachnang directed it from 1984 to 1991. Wikipedia states Francesco Manacorda has been director since 2024. The museum lists Marcella Beccaria as deputy director (Castello di Rivoli).

Building: first mentioned in 1159. Sacked by French troops. Filippo Juvarra intervened from 1716 but left the facade unfinished. The comune of Rivoli used it as barracks after 1863, and restoration began in 1979 (Wikipedia). The Manica Lunga is the only 17th-century part still visible (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Castello di Rivoli: Regione Piemonte, the Ministry of Culture, Compagnia di San Paolo, Fondazione CRC, Fondazione CRT and Intesa Sanpaolo

name: National Gallery of Jamaica
overview: National art museum at 12 Ocean Boulevard on the Kingston Waterfront, with a branch, National Gallery West, in Montego Bay (the gallery's own site). It describes itself as the largest and oldest public art museum in the English-speaking Caribbean and holds Jamaica's National Art Collection.

It is a division of the Institute of Jamaica, under the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport (the gallery's site). The Institute was established in 1879 by Governor Sir Anthony Musgrave (Wikipedia, Institute of Jamaica).

Opened on 22 November 1974 at Devon House with 237 paintings and drawings and 25 sculptures transferred from the Institute of Jamaica. It moved to the Roy West Building downtown in 1982 (Wikipedia). The Jamaica 55 government site dates the move to 1983 and says it was meant to be temporary.
funding_verdict: National Gallery of Jamaica: owned by the Government of Jamaica through the Institute of Jamaica, with CHASE and Tourism Enhancement Fund money for programmes and Scotiabank Jamaica as an exhibition partner

press_items.title: Annie Paul, "Mismanagement, machinations and more at the National Gallery of Jamaica..." (29 July 2014)
Matthew Hunte, "National Gallery of Jamaica Director Faces Accusations of Intimidating and Bullying Employees" (15 August 2014)

name: Aomori Museum of Art
overview: Prefectural art museum at 185 Chikano, Yasuta, Aomori City, next to the Sannai-Maruyama site, a Jomon-period settlement that is part of a World Heritage listing (museum English site; Wikipedia).
Established by Aomori Prefecture under the Aomori Prefectural Museum of Art Ordinance (Ordinance No. 69 of 2005). Opened on 13 July 2006 (museum site; prefectural ordinance).

Building by the architect Jun Aoki, shaped after the excavation trenches of the nearby site: white-painted brick over a ground cut into trenches, with white cube galleries beside galleries with exposed earthen floors and walls (museum site).
funding_verdict: Aomori Museum of Art: prefectural museum, established by Aomori Prefecture, with media and corporate supporters

name: Hakone Open-Air Museum
overview: Sculpture museum at 1121 Ninohira, Hakone, Kanagawa Prefecture (museum website).

The Chokoku no Mori Art and Culture Foundation says it was launched on 6 September 1968 as the Chokoku no Mori Museum foundation, that the museum opened on 1 August 1969 as Japan's first open-air museum devoted to sculpture, and that it became a public interest foundation on 1 April 2012 (foundation website, translated from Japanese). Japanese Wikipedia gives the opening as 6 September 1969.

The foundation says it was established by the Fujisankei Group, centred on Fuji Television, Sankei Shimbun and Nippon Broadcasting System (foundation website). The museum website names Nobutaka Shikanai as its founder and first director, who aimed to "contribute to the development of sculpture" because no museum devoted to sculpture existed in Japan. Japanese Wikipedia calls him chairman of the Fujisankei Group.
funding_verdict: Hakone Open-Air Museum: mainly self-funded: admission income, with donations and corporate sponsorship of the original construction

name: Pola Museum of Art
overview: Art museum at 1285 Sengokuhara, Hakone, Kanagawa Prefecture, in a forest with beeches more than 300 years old (museum website; e-flux directory).

It opened in September 2002 to show the collection of Suzuki Tsuneshi (鈴木常司, 1930 to 2000; e-flux spelling), son of Pola's founder and president of the cosmetics company for about 40 years, who died before it opened (museum website).
Collection: about 10,000 items gathered over some 40 years: Western painting, Japanese Western-style and Nihonga painting, prints, East Asian ceramics, glass and cosmetic tools (e-flux directory).
funding_verdict: Pola Museum of Art: private foundation: the Pola Art Foundation, built on the Pola founding family's fortune

name: Nara National Museum
overview: National museum at 50 Noborioji-cho, Nara City.
Established in 1889 as the Imperial Museum of Nara and opened to the public on 29 April 1895 (museum history page).
Renamed the Imperial Household Museum of Nara in 1900 and Nara National Museum in 1952.
funding_verdict: Nara National Museum: public: the National Institutes for Cultural Heritage, on Japanese government funding

name: Sapporo International Art Festival
overview: Triennial art festival in Sapporo that exhibits artworks and new forms of expression from around the world in museums, parks, public facilities, underground spaces, former theatres and snow storage facilities. Its Ainu-language name is Usa Mosir un Askay utar Sapporo otta Uekarpa (the festival's website).

Editions: summer in 2014 (19 July to 28 September, 72 days) and 2017 (6 August to 1 October), then winter in 2024 (20 January to 25 February, 37 days). The 2020 edition was cancelled because of COVID-19. The Secretariat acknowledges that some people felt the 2024 run was too short and calls it "the best possible outcome given SIAF's advantage in media art", with budget size and the winter season also shaping the decision (Festival Timing and Budget page).

SIAF2027, "Planet Snow" (upas mintar / upas nociw, Ainu words for "snow garden" and "snow star"), runs from 16 January to 21 February 2027 across 11 venues. Some venues have different dates: Sapporo Science Center from 5 January, the Hokkaido Museum of Modern Art from 9 January to 11 April (tentative), the Odori 500-m Underground Walkway Gallery from 16 January to 24 March, and the Sapporo Snow Festival Odori site from 4 to 21 February.
funding_verdict: Sapporo International Art Festival: city-organised: City of Sapporo, with support from the national Agency for Cultural Affairs, foundations and corporate partners

name: Hara Museum ARC
overview: Contemporary and traditional East Asian art museum at 2855-1 Kanai, Shibukawa, Gunma, on grounds adjacent to the Ikaho Green Bokujo recreational ranch (museum website, ART iT).

Operated by the Foundation Arc-en-Ciel, which Toshio Hara established in 1977 and chairs. The foundation opened the Hara Museum of Contemporary Art in Shinagawa, Tokyo, in 1979 and opened the ARC as an annex in 1988 (museum website).

The Tokyo museum, in a Western-style building first built as a residence in 1938, closed in January 2021. In a notice of November 2018 the foundation gave the age of the building, limits on accessibility and severe restrictions on reconstructing old buildings as its reasons (museum website, foundation notice on ART iT).
funding_verdict: Hara Museum ARC: foundation-run: the foundation set up by Toshio Hara, with membership fees and corporate supporting members

name: Artizon Museum
overview: Art museum at 1-7-2 Kyobashi, Chuo-ku, Tokyo, with galleries on three floors in the lower section of Museum Tower Kyobashi (e-flux, Artizon site). Its best-known holdings are Impressionist works and modern Japanese Western-style paintings (e-flux).
Founded as the Bridgestone Museum of Art by Ishibashi Shojiro, founder of Bridgestone, on the second floor of the Bridgestone Building in Kyobashi. It opened on 8 January 1952 (Artizon history page).
In 1956 Ishibashi established the Ishibashi Foundation, which took over the museum. In 1961 he gave the foundation most of his collection (Artizon history page).
funding_verdict: Artizon Museum: private foundation, operated by the Ishibashi Foundation, which the founder of Bridgestone set up in 1956
wider_context: Bridgestone's Firestone unit was sued on 17 November 2005 in a US federal court under the Alien Tort Statute by 23 Liberian children who worked on its rubber plantation in Liberia (International Rights Advocates).

The Seventh Circuit opinion, written by Judge Richard Posner and posted on 11 July 2011, left summary judgment for Firestone in place on the child-labour claims because the plaintiffs had not shown a sufficiently clear rule of customary international law on child labour, and held that corporations can be liable under the Alien Tort Statute (International Rights Advocates; Business and Human Rights Resource Centre).

Shojiro Ishibashi founded Bridgestone in 1931 and set up the Ishibashi Foundation, which runs the museum, in 1956; the museum was called the Bridgestone Museum of Art until it closed in 2015 (Artizon history and founder pages).

name: Japan Folk Crafts Museum (Nihon Mingeikan)
overview: Folk crafts museum at 4-3-33 Komaba, Meguro-ku, Tokyo, near Komaba-Todaimae Station on the Keio Inokashira Line (museum website, Wikipedia).
Planned in 1926 by Yanagi Soetsu (1889 to 1961) and others, and opened in 1936 in Komaba as the base of the Mingei (folk crafts) movement. Yanagi was its founding director (museum website).
Yanagi had earlier planned a private museum, the Shirakaba Museum, in 1917, opened the Korean Folk Art Museum in Seoul in 1924, and opened a Nihon Mingeikan in Hamamatsu in 1931 (museum website).
funding_verdict: Japan Folk Crafts Museum: public-interest foundation: admissions, membership dues and donations

name: NTT InterCommunication Center (ICC)
overview: Media art centre on the 4th floor of Tokyo Opera City Tower, 3-20-2 Nishishinjuku, Shinjuku, Tokyo. Hatsudai Station is about a 3-minute walk from the East exit (Tokyo Art Beat).

A cultural facility run by NTT East Corp. (stated by ICC). It opened on 19 April 1997 to mark 100 years of telephone service in Japan, after about eight years of preparation from 1990 (stated by ICC).
Building: a floor of the Tokyo Opera City Tower. Medosch (Telepolis, 15 August 2001) says ICC "has given up one floor" and the permanent collection on display shrank.
funding_verdict: NTT InterCommunication Center (ICC): corporate-run: NTT East, the telecom operator

name: Nezu Museum
overview: Museum of pre-modern Japanese and East Asian art at 6-5-1 Minami-Aoyama, Minato-ku, Tokyo, about a 10-minute walk from Omotesando Station (Exit B3, with an elevator) (museum visit page, Wikipedia).

Built on the private collection of Nezu Kaichiro (1860 to 1940). After his death a foundation was set up and began public exhibitions in 1941 (Wikipedia). Exhibitions resumed in 1946 after the collection was moved away from central Tokyo and escaped the May 1945 bombing (Wikipedia).
Nezu Kaichiro bought Ogata Korin's "Irises" screen in 1914. It is shown for a limited time each April and May, when the irises in the garden bloom (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Nezu Museum: private foundation: the Nezu collection, admissions and earned income
